text:
I need to write a reference letter. I manage a 400-cow dairy farm, and one of our workers, Tomás, is applying to the two-year agricultural technology program at the state technical college.

What I know about him:
- He's worked for us for 3 years, since he was 19.
- He runs the 3 a.m. milking shift on his own, 5 days a week.
- He learned our herd management software and now flags sick cows for the vet. Last winter he caught 9 cases of mastitis early.
- He left for 5 weeks in the middle of last summer when his father got sick in Mexico. He told me 2 days before he left.
- His written English is weaker than his spoken English. He's taking a night class for it.
- He has missed 2 shifts in 3 years, not counting those 5 weeks.

One page, from me as farm manager.

Before I draft this, a few questions. Your answers will change what the letter says:

1. **The 5-week absence and the written English.** Do you want either one in the letter? My suggestion: mention the English along with the night class, since the college will see his writing anyway and the night class reflects well on him. I'd leave out the absence unless the college asks about gaps or reliability. A family emergency, plus 2 missed shifts in 3 years, is a strong attendance record. What's your call?

2. **How he learned the software.** Did he take it on himself, or did you assign it? And do you know what catching those 9 mastitis cases early saved you, or what the vet said about it? Lost milk, treatment costs, cows you kept, anything like that? A concrete outcome is the most convincing thing a reference letter can include.

3. **What he wants after the program.** Does he plan to come back to your farm or go somewhere else in dairy? Would you hire him again, or promote him, once he finishes? "I would hire him back" carries a lot of weight with an admissions reader.

4. **Anything else you've seen yourself.** Has he trained newer workers, fixed a problem nobody asked him to fix, or been trusted with something beyond milking, like keys, calving, or equipment? Even one short story helps.

5. **The details.** I need his full name, your name, the farm's name and location, and who the letter goes to (an admissions committee or a named person). Also let me know if the college gave you a form or specific questions to answer.

If you don't know something, just say so and I'll write around it.

1. Go with what you said: mention the English and the night class, and leave out the absence. For what it's worth, before he left he got his cousin, who used to work for us, to cover his shifts, and he came back the day he said he would.

2. I'm not sure whether he took it on himself or I assigned it. The vet told us catching those mastitis cases early saved us about $8,000.

3. I don't know what he plans after the program. I can keep his job open part-time on weekends while he's in it.

4. Nothing beyond what I gave you, except that he failed the written test in a dairy safety course once and passed it the second time.

5. His full name is Tomás Reyes. I'm Mike Hollis, farm manager at Hollis Dairy. The letter goes through the college's online portal and is due February 1. I don't have a named person, and I don't know of any form or specific questions. The committee can call me at 555-0187.

Here's the letter. A few choices I made:

- **The failed safety test is not in the letter.** A failed written test would make the committee worry about his writing even more, and the night class already answers that worry. If you'd like to include it, one honest sentence would work: "He failed the written part of a dairy safety course once, studied, and passed it the second time."
- **The 5-week absence isn't mentioned.** But I did add one general line saying he finds his own cover when he needs time off. That's true because of what he did with his cousin, and it shows he's reliable without getting into the leave.
- **I didn't say who started the software work**, since you're not sure. The letter just says he learned it.
- **I left out a date and address block** because it's going through the portal. If the portal asks for a signed PDF, add the date and your signature at the bottom.

<final_document>
Dear Admissions Committee,

I am the farm manager at Hollis Dairy, a 400-cow operation, and I am writing to recommend Tomás Reyes for your two-year agricultural technology program. Tomás has worked for us for three years, since he was 19. He is one of the most dependable people I have employed.

Five days a week, Tomás runs our 3 a.m. milking shift on his own. There is no supervisor on the farm at that hour. I trust him with the whole herd and the parlor, and he has never given me a reason not to. In three years he has missed two shifts. When he has needed time off, he has arranged cover for his shifts himself before he came to me.

What makes him a strong fit for your program is the work he has done with our herd management software. Tomás learned the system and now uses it to flag sick cows for our veterinarian. Last winter he caught nine cases of mastitis early, and our vet estimates that saved the farm about $8,000. He watches the animals, reads the data, and connects the two. That is the kind of work your program trains people to do, and he is already doing it.

I'll be direct about one area where he is still growing. Tomás's spoken English is good, but his written English is weaker. He knows it, and he is doing something about it: he is taking a night English class on his own time, on top of a shift that starts at 3 a.m. That tells you how seriously he will take his coursework.

To support him while he studies, I will keep his job at Hollis Dairy open part-time on weekends for the length of the program.

I recommend Tomás without reservation. If you have any questions, please call me at 555-0187.

Sincerely,

Mike Hollis
Farm Manager, Hollis Dairy
</final_document>
